headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Male Circumcision
headings.content: Male circumcision is one of the oldest and most common surgical procedures globally, involving the surgical removal of the prepuce, or foreskin, which covers the glans penis. In the Nigerian context and across broader global communities, this practice is performed for a myriad of reasons, encompassing religious obligations, cultural traditions, and preventative health measures. As nursing students preparing for clinical practice and professional licensing exams, understanding male circumcision requires viewing the procedure through a holistic lens that integrates medical science with socio-cultural awareness. Historically and culturally, circumcision marks significant milestones such as initiation into adulthood or religious covenants in various Nigerian ethnic groups. From a public health perspective, international health organizations recognize the procedure as a vital biomedical intervention in reducing the transmission of certain sexually transmitted infections, including HIV. Nurses must approach the subject with cultural sensitivity, recognizing that family and community values heavily influence decisions regarding when and how the procedure is performed. Furthermore, professional nursing standards dictate that whether circumcision is performed on a neonate, child, or adult, the procedure must be executed in a sterile environment by trained practitioners to minimize risks and uphold patient dignity. Nurses serve as educators, advocates, and care coordinators, ensuring that the rights of the patient or their guardians are respected while promoting safe, evidence-based practices that prioritize the overall health and well-being of the individual.

headings.title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Male Genitalia
headings.content: A thorough grasp of the anatomy and physiology of the male genitalia is paramount for nurses caring for patients undergoing circumcision. The penis is principally composed of three cylindrical columns of erectile tissue: two dorsal corpora cavernosa and one ventral corpus spongiosum, which encloses the penile urethra. The distal end of the penis expands to form the glans penis, a sensitive structure that is normally protected by the prepuce or foreskin in uncircumcised males. The prepuce is a double-layered fold of skin and mucous tissue attached inferiorly to the urethral meatus by a delicate, highly vascular fold called the frenulum. Blood supply to the penis is rich, primarily derived from the internal pudendal artery branches, including the dorsal, deep, and bulbar arteries, which explains why surgical procedures in this area can result in significant bleeding if hemostasis is not meticulously managed. Innervation is equally extensive, provided by the dorsal nerve of the penis (a branch of the pudendal nerve) and the perineal nerves, supplying abundant sensory receptors that necessitate effective local or regional anesthesia during surgical intervention. Understanding these anatomical structures allows the nurse to anticipate potential complications, such as excessive bleeding from the frenular artery or trauma to the glans and urethra during the surgical procedure. Furthermore, recognizing normal developmental variations helps the nurse distinguish between typical anatomy and congenital anomalies, such as hypospadias or epispadias, which serve as absolute contraindications to routine circumcision.

headings.title: Indications and Contraindications for the Procedure
headings.content: Clinical decision-making regarding male circumcision requires a careful evaluation of indications and contraindications to ensure patient safety and positive health outcomes. Indications for the procedure vary across the lifespan. In neonates and infants, circumcision is often performed for cultural, religious, or preventative health preferences. In older boys and adult men, medical indications frequently arise, including phimosis (the inability to retract the foreskin over the glans), paraphimosis (a medical emergency where a retracted foreskin becomes trapped behind the glans and constricts blood flow), recurrent balanitis (inflammation of the glans), and chronic balanoposthitis (inflammation of both the glans and foreskin). Conversely, several absolute and relative contraindications must be meticulously screened for during the nursing assessment. The most critical absolute contraindication is the presence of congenital penile anomalies, such as hypospadias (where the urethral meatus opens on the ventral side of the penis) or epispadias, because the foreskin is often surgically required later to repair these defects. Other contraindications include bleeding disorders (such as hemophilia or severe coagulopathies), acute local infections, prematurity, or compromised systemic health status in newborns until they are medically stable. Nurses play a frontline role in reviewing patient histories, identifying these risk factors, and communicating findings to the surgical team to prevent severe adverse events.

headings.title: Preoperative Nursing Assessment and Preparation
headings.content: Comprehensive preoperative nursing assessment and preparation are critical components in minimizing surgical risks and ensuring a smooth perioperative course. For pediatric patients, the nurse must conduct a thorough health history review, checking for any family history of bleeding disorders, known drug allergies, and current medications. A complete physical examination must confirm that the infant is stable, feeding well, and free of systemic illness or localized skin infections in the diaper area. For adult patients, the assessment includes evaluating understanding of the procedure, obtaining informed consent (or parental consent for minors), and assessing anxiety levels. Preoperative preparation also involves ensuring appropriate fasting guidelines are followed if sedation or general anesthesia is required, although local anesthesia is standard for neonates. The nurse must verify that all baseline vital signs are recorded and that any required laboratory investigations, such as coagulation profiles for patients with suspected bleeding risks, are reviewed by the clinician. Patient and family education at this stage is vital; the nurse explains what will happen during and after the procedure, sets realistic expectations regarding pain management, and provides instructions on post-procedural hygiene. Finally, the nurse performs a safety checklist verification, confirming the patient's identity, the planned procedure, and the absence of contraindications right up to the moment the patient is transferred to the procedure room.

headings.title: Surgical Techniques and Equipment Used in Male Circumcision
headings.content: Various surgical techniques and specialized instruments are utilized in male circumcision, with the choice depending largely on the age of the patient and the clinician's expertise. For neonates and infants, the most common instruments include the Gomco clamp, the Plastibell device, and the Mogen clamp. The Gomco clamp functions by drawing the foreskin over a bell-shaped metal guard, applying a clamp to crush the blood vessels, and allowing the clinician to excise the foreskin with a scalpel while protecting the glans. The Plastibell is a plastic ring with a handle that is placed over the glans under the foreskin; a strong ligature string is tied tightly around the foreskin into a groove on the ring, cutting off blood supply so that the excess foreskin necroses and the plastic ring falls off naturally within 5 to 7 days. The Mogen clamp uses a shield mechanism to isolate and crush the foreskin before excision. For older children and adult males, circumcision is typically performed using traditional surgical dissection with a scalpel and scissors, where the foreskin is circumferentially incised and meticulously sutured with absorbable material to achieve precise hemostasis and cosmetic alignment. Nurses must be thoroughly familiar with the assembly, sterilization, and functioning of each device and instrument set. Having the correct equipment prepared and functioning flawlessly prevents delays during the procedure and ensures the highest standard of patient safety and surgical efficacy.

headings.title: Intraoperative Nursing Responsibilities and Safety
headings.content: Intraoperative nursing responsibilities are vital for maintaining a sterile, safe, and efficient environment throughout the circumcision procedure. Whether acting in a scrub or circulating role, the nurse must strictly adhere to aseptic techniques to prevent surgical site infections, which are particularly hazardous given the sensitive anatomical location. Before the procedure begins, the nurse assists with patient positioning—typically supine with limbs gently secured or restrained in infants to prevent accidental movement that could cause trauma. The nurse prepares the surgical field using appropriate antiseptic solutions (such as chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine, taking care to avoid skin irritation or chemical burns in neonates) and drapes the patient accordingly. During the administration of local anesthesia, such as a dorsal penile nerve block or a ring block using lidocaine (without epinephrine to prevent ischemic necrosis), the nurse provides supportive care, monitors the patient's physiological responses, and offers comforting measures such as non-nutritive sucking or oral sucrose for infants. Throughout the surgery, the nurse maintains an accurate count of instruments, needles, and gauze sponges, monitors the sterile field for contamination, and assists the surgeon by handing equipment or managing suction. Immediate post-incision, the nurse remains vigilant, observing for signs of excessive bleeding or adverse reactions to anesthetics, and ensures that all waste and sharps are disposed of safely in accordance with standard universal precautions.

headings.title: Postoperative Nursing Care and Pain Management
headings.content: Postoperative nursing care and meticulous pain management are essential for ensuring comfort, promoting rapid healing, and preventing complications after a circumcision. Immediately following the procedure, the nurse monitors vital signs and assesses the surgical site frequently—every 15 minutes for the first hour, then progressively less often as stability is confirmed. The primary focus of the initial assessment is checking for hemorrhage, ensuring that the urinary meatus is unobstructed, and confirming that the patient is able to void normally. Pain management is tailored to the patient's age and pain scale; neonates benefit from non-pharmacological methods like soothing and cuddling, combined with prescribed analgesics such as acetaminophen or topical anesthetic creams when appropriate, while older children and adults may require prescribed oral analgesics. The nurse instructs patients or caregivers on proper wound care, which typically involves keeping the area clean and dry, applying a light layer of petroleum jelly (vaseline) to the glans to prevent the wound from adhering to diapers or clothing, and avoiding harsh soaps or scrubbing. If a Plastibell device was used, the nurse explains that the plastic ring will detach on its own within a week and that caregivers should never attempt to pull or yank the ring off prematurely. By addressing both physical comfort and educational needs, the nurse empowers caregivers to manage the recovery phase confidently at home.

headings.title: Potential Complications and Emergency Management
headings.content: Although male circumcision is generally considered a safe and routine procedure, nurses must remain vigilant for potential complications and be fully prepared for emergency management. The most frequent immediate complication is hemorrhage or excessive bleeding from the surgical incision line or the frenular artery, which requires prompt intervention such as applying direct gentle pressure with sterile gauze and notifying the surgeon for potential suture ligation. Another acute complication is acute urinary retention, which can result from localized edema, tight bandaging, or pain-induced sphincter spasm; nurses must monitor for the time of the first post-procedure void and report any inability to urinate. Infection is a risk that can manifest as increasing redness, swelling, purulent discharge, or foul odor days after the procedure. In rare instances, severe surgical mishaps can occur, including inadvertent amputation of the glans, severe penile shaft injury, or urethral fistula formation, which constitute major surgical emergencies requiring immediate specialist urological intervention. Additionally, if a Plastibell device slips proximally or is left on too long without falling off, it can cause severe strangulation and edema of the glans, necessitating urgent clinical removal. By maintaining high vigilance, performing serial assessments, and recognizing deviations from normal recovery trajectories early, the nurse plays a life-saving role in mitigating adverse outcomes.

headings.title: Patient Education and Discharge Instructions
headings.content: Patient education and comprehensive discharge instructions are the final critical steps in ensuring safe, uninterrupted recovery after male circumcision. The nurse must provide clear, concise, and culturally appropriate verbal and written instructions to the patient or parents before discharge. Education must cover expected healing milestones, such as mild swelling and yellowish exudate (which is a normal part of the granulation and healing process and should not be mistaken for pus or infection). Caregivers need explicit guidance on hygiene practices, including how to clean the area gently with warm water, how to change diapers frequently to prevent irritation from urine and stool, and how to apply prescribed barrier ointments or petroleum jelly. The nurse must also educate families on warning signs that require immediate contact with healthcare providers or return to the emergency department, such as continuous or spurting bleeding, spreading redness, fever, foul-smelling discharge, or complete inability to urinate for several hours. For older boys and adult patients, discharge instructions should also address activity restrictions, such as avoiding strenuous physical exercise, cycling, or sexual activity until the wound is fully healed, as advised by the clinician. By equipping patients and caregivers with this essential knowledge, nurses promote adherence to care plans, reduce anxiety, and foster optimal recovery outcomes across communities in Nigeria and beyond.
